mcqs.question: You need to split an 1,800-line migration to a new pricing service into reviewable PRs. What makes a split good?
options: Split by file type — models in one PR, controllers in another, tests in a third
Split by author — each engineer opens a PR for the part they wrote
Split roughly evenly by line count so no PR exceeds 400 lines
Split so each PR is independently mergeable and safe to deploy alone, even if it changes no behavior yet
mcqs.explanation: Deployability is the constraint that makes a split real: adding the new client as unused code, then the flag, then the wiring, then the flip, each merges on its own and each asks the reviewer one question. Splitting by file type or line count produces PRs that are individually meaningless and can't ship without the others, so the reviewer still has to hold the whole change in their head.

mcqs.question: Which single line in a PR description saves a reviewer the most time on a 400-line diff?
options: "The real logic is in `PriceCache.get`; the other 300 lines are generated protobuf."
"All tests pass and coverage is unchanged."
"Please review by Thursday, this is blocking the release."
"Refactors the pricing module for clarity and maintainability."
mcqs.explanation: Reviewers open a large diff with no idea which lines carry the risk, so pointing at the 40 that matter converts a skim into a focused read — and it is the sentence almost nobody writes. CI already reports test status, a deadline changes priority but not reading speed, and a generic summary restates what the diff already shows.

mcqs.question: Your team wants every schema migration seen by a DBA. What's the most robust way to guarantee it?
options: Add a checklist item to the PR template asking the author to confirm DBA review
Ask engineers in standup to tag the DBA team whenever they touch SQL
Have the DBA team subscribe to repository notifications and watch for migration files
Add a `CODEOWNERS` rule mapping `*.sql` paths to the DBA team, backed by a branch protection rule requiring owner approval
mcqs.explanation: CODEOWNERS plus required-owner approval makes the merge physically impossible without a DBA, which encodes the rule as configuration rather than as something a tired engineer remembers on a Friday. Templates, verbal conventions and notification-watching all depend on a human doing the right thing at the moment they're most likely not to.

mcqs.question: A team can only commit to one review SLA number. Which one should it be?
options: Number of PRs each engineer reviews per week
First response within 4 business hours, even if the response is "looking this afternoon"
Final approval within 24 hours
Zero PRs open longer than one week
mcqs.explanation: It's the unbounded wait that does the damage — not knowing when a review will come is what pushes an author to start a third parallel branch and lose all their context. A 24-hour approval target is weaker on the dimension that hurts, a one-week bound tolerates exactly the stalls you're trying to kill, and per-engineer review counts measure activity rather than flow.

mcqs.question: A team raises its policy from one required approver to two and finds defects still reach production at the same rate. What's the most likely explanation?
options: Two approvers takes longer, so reviewers rush and skip the tests
The defects are in code paths that no reviewer has permission to see
Diffusion of responsibility — each approver reads less carefully assuming the other one was thorough
Two approvals only helps if both reviewers are senior engineers
mcqs.explanation: Social loafing is the well-documented cost of adding approvers: shared responsibility reduces each individual's felt ownership, so two shallow reads replace one careful one. That's why the usual answer is one required approver by default with a second specific owner added by CODEOWNERS only on high-blast-radius paths, rather than a blanket rule.

mcqs.question: PRs assigned to a whole team routinely sit untouched for days. What fixes it most reliably?
options: Ask authors to post in the team channel when a PR has been waiting a day
Reduce the required approver count from two to one
Add a bot that auto-approves PRs open longer than 48 hours
Auto-assign one named human per PR via round-robin, plus a bot that pings at 48 hours
mcqs.explanation: The stall is diffusion of responsibility — nobody refused, nobody was asked — so the fix is putting the request in exactly one person's queue and making the reminder structural instead of something the author has to do socially. Auto-approval removes review entirely, fewer approvers doesn't help when the problem is that zero people started, and asking authors to nag leaves the polite ones blocked longest.
